strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical question: how ridge regularization affects performative learning, especially in repeated risk minimization where estimation-based methods are impractical.

The theoretical development is substantial and rigorous for the stated settings: it characterizes the performative fixed point, excess risk, and optimal ridge in the population regime (Theorem 1, Corollary 2), and derives a deterministic equivalent for the risk in the proportional regime (Theorem 3).

The overparameterized analysis yields a nontrivial and interesting phenomenology: the optimal regularization direction depends on noise level and feature type, and performativity that reinforces existing trends can improve optimally regularized risk (Theorem 4).

The paper connects to several relevant literatures (performative prediction, high-dimensional ridge regression, spurious correlations) and builds appropriately on existing tools (Han and Xu, 2023; Ildiz et al., 2025).
The synthetic experiments in Figures 1-3 provide good support for the theory, including matching theoretical curves and the predicted sign changes with noise.
The real-data experiments on Housing and LSAC illustrate the population-regime predictions and show the qualitative behavior of the optimal ridge under synthetic performative shifts.
Limitations are largely acknowledged: Gaussian/linear assumptions, synthetic performative shifts, and the need for future work on more complex data/models.
Ethical considerations are touched upon via long-term fairness and bias amplification, and the experimental details are documented in Appendix D.
weaknesses: The population analysis permits negative optimal regularization (Corollary 2), but the RRM fixed-point convergence in Lemma 5 requires the spectral radius of (Sigma + lambda I)^-1 Sigma D to be below 1. Negative lambda can violate this condition, so the fixed point may not be reached, yet the paper does not restrict lambda or discuss stability. This makes the population optimal-regularization claim potentially invalid in parts of the parameter space.

The optimal lambda in the population regime is obtained by minimizing a first-order approximation with remainder O(||F||_op^2). The paper argues empirically that the approximation is accurate near the optimum, but it does not prove that the approximate minimizer is close to the true minimizer, nor does it quantify the error in the resulting lambda and risk.

The high-dimensional phenomenology in Theorem 4 is derived only for the special covariance Sigma = [[I, rho I], [rho I, I]] with small rho and to first order in mean performative effects b_bar and c_bar. It does not analyze variance in the entries of D in the overparameterized setting, even though variance is shown to matter in the population setting. The abstract's broad claims about 'overall strength' are therefore narrower than stated.

The real-data validation of the overparameterized theory is questionable: Figure 4c uses LSAC with n=100 and d=22, so p/n<1 (underparameterized), while Theorem 3 assumes kappa=p/n>1. Thus the experiment does not actually test the overparameterized regime it claims to support; the synthetic Figure 3 is the only proper test of Theorem 4.

The paper does not provide a practical way to set the regularization in anticipation of performative effects: the formulas depend on unknown quantities such as b_bar, sigma, kappa, and rho, but no estimation or robust-selection procedure is given, despite the abstract implying practical guidance.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of code in the submission. The reproducibility statement says 'The code is available at' without a link, and Appendix D says the code will be released only upon acceptance, which is insufficient for reviewers to verify the experiments.

The empirical evaluation is limited: only two real datasets, no comparison to alternative mitigation or estimation methods, no real performative data, and no real-data tests for negative performative effects or for the role of spurious features c.

The presentation has some overstatements and minor formatting/typographical issues (e.g., reference formatting and a few garbled equations in the PDF text), which make it harder to assess the exact scope of the guarantees.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of ridge regularization in performative linear regression, covering both population and proportional high-dimensional regimes.
Derives a clean closed-form expression for the optimal regularization in the population regime, showing it scales with the mean performative effect (Corollary 2).
Establishes a deterministic equivalent for the excess risk at the performative fixed point in the over-parameterized regime (Theorem 3), enabling analysis of optimal regularization.

Reveals a novel phenomenology: in the over-parameterized regime, the direction of the optimal regularization shift depends on the noise level (Theorem 4), and performativity can improve the optimally-regularized risk when it reinforces existing trends.
Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data and two real datasets (Housing, LSAC) qualitatively support the theoretical predictions.
weaknesses: The population analysis allows negative optimal regularization (Corollary 2), but the convergence proof for RRM (Lemma 5) only guarantees convergence for λ ≥ 0; for negative λ the iteration may diverge. Thus the negative optimal λ may not be attainable, undermining the practical relevance of this result.

The over-parameterized deterministic equivalent (Theorem 3) is for the estimator after two iterations, not the true fixed point, and relies on an unquantified O(||D||_op^2) approximation. The error bound is not made explicit, and the main theorem is not empirically validated—Figure 3 shows only qualitative shifts, not quantitative agreement with R_eq.
The proof of Theorem 3 adapts results for ridgeless/min-norm interpolators (Han & Xu, 2023) to ridge regression; the extension is not fully detailed and may have gaps, raising soundness concerns.

Practical utility is limited: the performative parameters (\bar b, \bar c) are unknown, and the paper provides no estimation procedure, yet the abstract/conclusion claim it is possible to 'set the regularization in anticipation' of the performative effect.

Experiments are weak: they use synthetic performative shifts on real data, no comparison to baselines or other performative learning methods, no fairness evaluation despite the stated motivation, and only two datasets. The over-parameterized theory is not quantitatively tested.
Reproducibility is insufficient: the code is not provided (only promised upon acceptance), and the reproducibility statement is incomplete.
The over-parameterized analysis assumes a specific block covariance structure and small ρ, limiting generality. The paper does not discuss these limitations in a dedicated section.
The paper overclaims in the abstract and conclusion relative to what is actually demonstrated.

strengths: Provides a timely and novel theoretical study of ridge regularization in performative learning, connecting performative prediction with high-dimensional ridge regression and random matrix theory.

The population analysis (Theorem 1, Corollary 2) gives a clean first-order risk expansion and an explicit optimal regularization formula λ* ∝ \bar{b}, revealing when zero excess risk is achievable and how spurious features affect the risk.

The over-parameterized analysis (Theorem 3, Theorem 4) establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point and characterizes how optimal regularization and optimally-regularized risk scale with performative strength, including the interesting finding that performativity can improve the optimal risk when it reinforces existing trends.
The appendix contains detailed proofs, explicit expansions, sign analyses (e.g., Lemmas 12–15), and convergence/error bounds, demonstrating substantial technical depth.
Synthetic experiments in Figure 3 support the over-parameterized theory, and real-data experiments on Housing/LSAC qualitatively illustrate the population and small-sample behaviors.

Reproducibility is partially addressed via a reproducibility statement, detailed preprocessing in Appendix D, and an explicit LLM-usage disclosure; limitations and future directions are discussed in the conclusions.
weaknesses: The practical message that regularization can be set “in anticipation” of performative effects is not operationalized: the optimal λ formulas depend on the unknown performative parameters b and c, and no estimation or robust selection procedure is provided.

The real-data experiment claimed to probe the over-parameterized regime (LSAC, n=100, p=22) is not actually over-parameterized because p<n; it therefore does not directly validate Theorem 3/4 and may instead reflect small-sample/population-like behavior.

The optimal-regularization results rely on local expansions (small ||F||, small ρ, small \bar{b},\bar{c}) and first-order approximations; there is no uniform guarantee that minimizing the approximation yields near-optimal true risk for moderate or large performative effects.

Negative optimal regularization in the population setting may not be implementable with standard ridge regression; although noted, the paper does not address constrained (λ≥0) selection or its consequences.

The role of the spurious performative parameter c is only higher order, and its claimed effect can be dominated by O(\bar{b}ρ²) approximation error, limiting the practical significance of the corresponding sign results.
Reproducibility of the empirical results is incomplete: the code URL is blank and the statement says code will be released only upon acceptance.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive—Gaussian features, label-only performative shift, linear model, diagonal D, and a specific block covariance—so the conclusions may not directly extend to strategic feature manipulation or nonlinear settings.

The abstract/introduction slightly overstate generality: “optimal regularization scales with overall strength” obscures the noise-dependent sign reversal in the over-parameterized regime, and the “set regularization in anticipation” claim is not supported without knowledge of b.

strengths: The paper combines performative learning with high-dimensional ridge regression and provides the first high-dimensional statistical analysis of regularization under performative effects, addressing a timely and practically relevant problem.

The population analysis is rigorous and interpretable: Lemma B.1 gives an explicit convergence rate to the performative fixed point, Theorem 4.1 gives a first-order excess-risk approximation, and Corollary 4.2 shows that the optimal ridge parameter scales with the mean performative strength \bar{b} and depends on spurious correlations through a Schur complement.

The over-parameterized analysis is technically substantial. Theorem 5.1 establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point using random-matrix tools, and Theorem 5.2 yields explicit expansions showing that the direction of the optimal regularization depends on the noise level and that the optimally regularized risk can improve when performativity reinforces existing trends.

The empirical section goes beyond a single setting: synthetic Gaussian experiments, two real-world datasets (Housing, LSAC), and a neural-network strategic-classification experiment qualitatively support the main theoretical findings. The paper also tests dropout, Lasso, and elastic net, suggesting the qualitative behavior is not limited to ridge regression.

The manuscript includes a thoughtful impact statement and limitations discussion, including the tension between evaluating on the initial versus shifted distribution, and it is clear about the label-shift-only nature of the performative model.
The presentation is generally well organized, with the main theoretical results stated clearly and the appendix providing detailed derivations.
weaknesses: The over-parameterized theorem analyzes only two RRM iterations and controls the error by \delta + O(\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2). Since Assumption 3.1 only requires \|b\|_\infty,\|c\|_\infty < 1, the O(\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2) term can be non-negligible, so the claim that the risk has reached a fixed point after two iterations is an approximation rather than a general exact statement.

Theorem 5.2 is derived under a highly simplified covariance structure (\Sigma = [[I_d, \rho I_d],[\rho I_d, I_d]]) with small \rho, diagonal D, and local expansions in \bar{b} and \bar{c}. The sign conditions also require \kappa \geq 2 in places. Thus the 'remarkable phenomenology' is established only in a restricted asymptotic regime, not for general high-dimensional performative learning.

The population optimal regularization in Corollary 4.2 is allowed to be negative (\lambda \in \mathbb{R}), but the RRM convergence argument relies on \|T\|_{\mathrm{op}} < 1, which may fail for negative \lambda. The paper acknowledges negative regularization but does not fully reconcile this with the convergence and positive-definiteness requirements of ridge regression.

The real-data experiment intended to illustrate the over-parameterized regime (LSAC with n=100) does not satisfy the theoretical requirement p/n = \kappa > 1: with d=22 (or p=44 if features are doubled), p/n < 1. Therefore Figure 4(c) does not actually test the proportional over-parameterized setting of Theorem 5.1, weakening the claimed empirical support for the over-parameterized theory.

The performative model is restricted to label shifts with features independent of \theta. Strategic behavior in practice often involves feature manipulation, and the paper only argues that global feature shifts can be absorbed by centering. This limits the external validity of the theoretical results.

Reproducibility is compromised by the incomplete code link: the manuscript says the code is available at 'https://github.com/' without a repository path, preventing independent verification of the experiments.

Some notation is inconsistent or confusing (e.g., \tilde{b} in Theorem 4.1 versus \bar{b} in Corollary 4.2 and later), and the dense derivations in the main text may be difficult for non-specialists to follow.

The theoretical machinery is adapted from existing high-dimensional regression and knowledge-distillation results (Han and Xu, 2023; Ildiz et al., 2025); the novelty lies mainly in the application to performative learning rather than in fundamentally new technical tools.

strengths: The paper opens a worthwhile direction by studying ridge regularization in performative learning through the lens of high-dimensional statistics. The population analysis (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2) is clean and shows that the optimal ridge penalty is proportional to the mean performative effect, with an explicit residual-risk expression.

Theorem 5.1 establishes a deterministic equivalent for the performative fixed point in the proportional regime, adapting high-dimensional ridge tools to performative repeated risk minimization. The resulting phenomenology in Theorem 5.2—e.g., the noise-dependent sign of the optimal regularization shift and the improved optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends—is novel and interesting.
The paper includes synthetic experiments that match the theory well, plus real-data and neural-network experiments, and it contains a thoughtful limitations and impact discussion.
weaknesses: The overparameterized results are highly local: they are first-order in bbar, cbar, and rho, with O(b^2+c^2) and O(rho^4) remainders, and assume diagonal D, a specific block covariance, small performative effects, and only two RRM iterations. The central claim that optimal regularization scales with the performative strength is therefore only an approximate local statement, not a general practical prescription.

The LSAC experiment with n=100 and d=22 (so p=44 if p=2d) is not in the overparameterized regime required by Theorem 5.1, which assumes p/n = kappa > 1. Thus Figure 4(c) cannot validate the proportional-regime theory; it is in the underparameterized regime, and the claimed agreement with the large-noise prediction is unsupported.

The real-data experiments do not match the theoretical setup: they do not construct spurious features with zero true coefficients, they only vary b and ignore c, and they choose performative features somewhat arbitrarily. The neural-network experiment uses a different strategic-classification performative model, so it provides only qualitative, not theoretical, support.
The code link is incomplete ('https://github.com/'), which harms reproducibility and makes it difficult to verify the empirical claims.

The paper overclaims practical impact. It does not provide a way to estimate the performative strength or covariance, yet the abstract and introduction suggest it is possible to set regularization in anticipation of performative effects. No comparison to existing performative mitigation methods is provided.

Most of the main analysis evaluates risk on D(theta=0) rather than the induced distribution D(theta). Although the authors justify this for fairness reasons, it is non-standard for performative prediction and limits the scope of the conclusions.

The real-data experiments do not report experimental uncertainty (e.g., error bars or number of independent runs), and the synthetic experiments use dimensions and sample sizes that are far from the asymptotic regime, making the empirical support weaker than claimed.

strengths: Provides the first high-dimensional statistical analysis of performative learning, deriving a deterministic equivalent for the performative fixed point in the proportional regime (Theorem 5.1) and optimal regularization scaling laws (Theorem 5.2), with detailed proofs in the appendices.

Population analysis (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2) cleanly shows that optimal ridge regularization is proportional to the mean performative strength \bar{b}, and that spurious performative effects enter only at higher order; these predictions are supported by synthetic figures.

Over-parameterized analysis reveals an interesting and nontrivial phenomenology: the optimal regularization moves in the same direction as the performative effect for low noise, but in the opposite direction for high noise, and the optimally regularized risk improves when performativity reinforces existing trends (B2 <= 0).
The paper also analyzes evaluation on the shifted distribution in Appendix F, providing a balanced treatment of both evaluation regimes and showing contrasting behavior for optimal risk.

Empirical evaluations on synthetic data, Housing/LSAC, and neural networks qualitatively support the theory, and additional experiments with dropout, Lasso, and elastic net suggest the findings are not tied only to ridge regression.
The manuscript is generally well-written and structured, with a clear impact statement and an honest discussion of the limitations of the performative label-shift model.
weaknesses: The theoretical model is restrictive: it assumes only label shift of the form y = x^T \theta_pop^* + x^T D\theta + w, with diagonal D, linear regression, squared loss, and no feature shifts or nonlinear performative effects. This limits the generality of the conclusions.

The population optimal regularization in Corollary 4.2 can be negative, but the convergence/fixed-point analysis for repeated risk minimization may break down for negative \lambda (e.g., the spectral-radius condition on T can fail). The paper does not discuss this stability issue, which could make the recommended negative regularization impractical.

The over-parameterized deterministic equivalent in Theorem 5.1 has error O(||D||_op^2) and relies on only two RRM iterations, so the approximation may degrade when the performative effect is strong. No quantitative bound is given for when the approximation is accurate.

The expansion in Theorem 5.2 is linear in \bar{b} and \bar{c} and assumes small \rho, ignoring the variance of the entries of b and c. The population analysis shows that such variance can strongly affect optimal risk, so the over-parameterized theory does not cover an important aspect of performativity.

The real-data experiments claimed to illustrate the proportional regime (LSAC with n=100 and d=22) do not actually satisfy p > n if p = 2d = 44, so they do not directly validate Theorem 5.1's over-parameterized setting. The synthetic experiments do, but the real-data evidence is weaker than the text implies.
Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete code link ('https://github.com/') in the manuscript, making independent verification of the experiments difficult.

The first-order population approximation underlying Corollary 4.2 may be inaccurate when the entries of b have high variance, precisely the regime where the excess risk is largest; although a second-order approximation is given, the main optimal-regularization formula is first-order.
